The newly hatched chick displays minimal locomotor capacity and depends entirely on brooding adults for thermoregulation during the first several days post-hatching. This neonatal mass is among the lowest recorded for emberizid sparrows, comparable to values reported for the closely related field sparrow and consistent with the general pattern among small-bodied North American passerines whereby reduced hatchling mass is offset by accelerated growth trajectories during the nestling period, enabling chicks to achieve the skeletal and feather development necessary for fledging within a relatively compressed developmental window.

Sexual dimorphism in body mass is minimal in this species, with males and females overlapping extensively in size, although breeding females may temporarily achieve slightly greater mass during egg production. The adult mass is consistent with the species' insectivorous-granivorous diet and its adoption of a high-metabolic-rate lifestyle characteristic of small aerial foragers.
